EDITED: After a few comments in this review, I will add a few points that I didn’t mention before, making it more complete (I will also correct a few grammar mistakes that I made).

Is this a good game? Yes!
Is it better than One Piece Pirate Warriors 3?? Absolutely no!
Is it worth it? Even if you are a One Piece fan, I have my doubts

Pirate Warriors 4 has a few positive aspects over PW3. Better graphics, new characters, the possibility to choose from several skills/moves and a few more (and new) missions. But that's it. Nothing more!

There are ONLY SIX arcs ([spoiler]Alabasta arc, the Enies Lobby arc, the Marineford arc, the New World Saga arc, the Whole Cake Island arc, and a game exclusive Wano arc. The Sabaody Archipelago arc is included in the Marineford arc, and Dressrosa arc is included in the New World Saga arc[/spoiler]).  Bandai had just ONE job: explore the Yonko saga. They didn't even manage to do it properly. There is no Zou Arc. There is no Reverie Arc. The lack of the old arcs and the poorly explored Yonko Saga disappointed me. The only thing new in here is the Whole Cake Island Arc and a poorly made Wano Country Arc.
They separated those 6 arcs in different missions. 5 of those missions are an easy 1x1 fight. Bandai should've put them inside a long mission, e.g. a final boss battle, like they did in PW3. Bandai chose to have more cutscenes (explaining 2/3 of the anime that weren't in the game) and less gameplay. Bandai randomly chose a few arcs to make them playable and the rest (the most part of the anime) to be cutscenes.
It took me a long time to get along with the combat camera. I just didn't like it. 
There are a few situations where you will experience a few bugs (Usopp's barrels don't stay in stairs, ally stuck inside a destroyed building for a long time, ranged characters have trouble to attack enemies that are on different heights, one of Luffy’s air attack send you flying above buildings, missing everything, etc.). There is also a bug where an enemy stay stuck above you (when you are close to the wall or the edge of the map) with a “falling animation”, even if you aren’t doing anything. You can attack it for free for a long time.
THERE IS NO DREAM LOG!! PW3 story mode was incredible. It was very exciting to remember the whole anime. But after getting an S on all missions, you could still have a lot of fun in Dream Log. Too bad, no dream log in here.
Besides that, there is not a single reason for getting an S-rank on all missions (and to complete the gallery) in PW4. You don’t get any reward, any achievement, nothing! The new mission rank system is completely useless.
"New characters". Nice, right? F* no!!!! Why will I want to play with all Sanji's brothers?? Where is Moria? Perona? Eneru? Garp? Kuma?!? ([spoiler] In PW4 you battle against Garp and Kuma but you can't play with them. [/spoiler]).
Don’t get me wrong. It was funny playing with some new characters. The thing I hated the most was the lack of characters that you could play with in PW3. There are a lot of characters that you see their development and growing in the anime and you don't even have a chance to play in PW4 because more than 2/3 of the anime are just cutscenes.
I won’t say anything about the online system, because I played the whole game solo. But you can read a few reviews saying that it is bugged and poorly implemented.
Bandai don't want you to struggle to get S ranks on all missions (as I said, it’s useless). They've made an easy and short game where you'll play only once the story mode, and if you want to have all the achievements, just play a few more missions of the Treasure Log. 
What about Free log? Pointless.
There isn’t any struggling point in PW4. Despite replaying a few missions, I completed the story mode in a few hours.

I've spent 130 hours on PW3 getting 100% of it. 
It took me just 29 hours on PW4, and I think I'll never touch it again.

I can't recommend a game that explores less than 1/3 of the anime.
It would be better if Whole Cake Island arc and Wano arc were launched for PW3 as a DLC.
They could have included ALL arcs on PW4. Too bad :(
It just seems like an unfinished game.
It really makes you feel like you're playing as one piece characters, i kept getting lost while i was playing as Zoro

This game is worth having as a One Piece fan and it`s a pretty decent musou game in general though it`s not without its flaws.

Pros

- Much better roster than Pirate Warriors 3, and the characters feel quite distinct. Additions like Kid, Hawkins, Reiju, and
  Carrot are lots of fun to play.

- Kaido's Dragon Form (and the Yonko in general) are insanely powerful and fun to play

- Better controller support than Pirate Warriors 3 but still requires some tweaking

- Pretty good quality cutscenes and animations

Cons

- Abridged story is hard to follow for beginners. Lots of important characters and side-plots are glossed over entirely. This 
  is definitely not how you want to get introduced to One Piece's story.

- The game content feels more sparse than Pirate Warriors 3. I should have 100% achievements and gotten S class finishes 
   on all missions (Story and Treasure Log) by about 35hrs in. Learning to use the entire roster will obviously add more time
   but I can't really see myself playing this for more than 70hrs in total if that.

- Camera is very slightly improved over Pirate Warriors but still pretty bad in general.

- The HUD gets cluttered very quickly and the minimap gets lit up like a Christmas tree which can make navigation a real 
   pain. 


Overall, I'd still recommend owning this game but don't buy it at full price. Wait for at least a 20-30% discount, and that's only if you're a One Piece fan. If you're new to the series or just like musou games, wait for something more steep like half off.

The good:
+ Gameplay and new movesets for many characters feel more fluent and devastating than PW3.
+ New giant type enemies are fun to fight.
+ The biggest roster of playable characters with 43 in the base game and 9 DLC.
+ New, bigger maps with the new building-destruction mechanic really help sell the power fantasy.
+ Better visual and effect when compared to PW3.
+ Great music.

The bad:
- Lock-on camera is god awful at times
- Many playable story arcs like Arlong, Thriller park, Fishman island in PW3, are either removed or reduced into recap cutscenes in PW4.
- With the revamped gameplay, the kizuna rush mechanic is gone, I can't say if this is for the better or worse in term of gameplay but without it, a somewhat unique aspect of characters' interactions is gone.
- Less alternate outfits for many characters.
- Dream logs' interface is severely downgraded from an interactive map to a simple selection menu.
- No more treasure events, legend diary or anything that would encourage you to replay story missions except for getting S grade.
- Some maps can be quite annoying to navigate.
- The new buildings-destruction system feel somewhat underused, like i was hoping to be able to create new routes on some maps and not just dealing extra damage to enemies.

Overall:
- Is this a good musou game? Yes.
- Is this game a good sequel to PW3? Absolutely not, if anything this is more PW3.5 than a full sequel.
- Should you try this out knowing nothing about One piece? Maybe not, many of the main story arcs are greatly abridged or glossed over.
- Should you try this out as a One Piece fan? Yes, but i highly recommend getting this on sale.

Pros
+ Dash Cancels, Air Combos and Big Damage to the Environment
+ Great Character Models
+ Mega-Church of Katakuri Approved
+ Co-op is Solid
+ Big Mom and Kaido are BIG!!!
+ It has that Lego Star Wars vibe of defeating a boss, and then getting to Free Play as them.
+ BIG MONKE LUFFY VS GIANT LIZARD KAIDO is a good final battle for this game.

Cons
- This game skips a few arcs (Skypiea, Fishman Island, pretty much all of East Blue.) It does recap events that aren't playable, and focuses more on the major battles within the series.
- This game is also really quick to beat your first time through, and there isn't much replay value outside of mastering different characters and 
- The Boss Armor is ANNOYING! It only pads out the fight, and can easily break the flow of combat when it recharges. Not as big of an issue in the late game, but by that point it's a grind to surpass.
- Invisible Walls where you think you should be able to jump, and the maps tend to be bigger than needed - especially when a mission-important ally needs help from the other side of the battlefield.
- I miss the Crew Attacks from 3... being able to have the crew line up and unleash a Combination Finisher on the Bosses really hyped-up the fights.

OVERALL
Gameplay - B (Only repetitive if you don't do combos on the plot important enemies. There is a lot of impact with the Supers, but you do have to grind in order to start One Punch styling on enemies. Controls feel good, Camera never fights, but the boss battle armor can get annoying if you aren't learning air combo tech.)
Story - EH (Watch/Read One Piece, this game doesn't flesh out all the characters)
Music - SSS (I highly enjoyed the remix of the returning OST in this game series.)
Graphics - Anime +

BOTTOM LINE
If you are already a fan of One Piece, and enjoy the Warrior-style gameplay... then I recommend giving this installment a try. I still recommend 3 as the starting point of the Pirate Wars series, since 1 and 2 were just full-priced Betas back in the day. For a PROPER One Piece game experience, I still want a game where you sail around and can fully explore islands - needs more inspiration from Black Flag and the Caribbean in KH3, or even P5S!

Wano Arc is not the same as in the manga/anime, but that's fine because the game-exclusive Wano Arc was still very enjoyable to go through.

The character roster is quite large, adding up to 43 current characters, and of course the 9 upcoming DLC characters. Katakuri and the Vinsmoke brothers being unlockable through gameplay so you don't have to purchase the season pass yet. I would recommend waiting until they announce the DLC characters and then picking up whoever you like. However, personally, I got the season pass because I want to have all the characters regardless.

The combat is incredible. I've played many Musou games in my life, (including but not limited to: Dynasty Warriors 1 through 7, the previous Pirate Warriors games, and the Berserk Musou game), and I have to say this game is one of the best demonstrations of how fun and engaging the Musou battle system is. I feel a rush of adrenaline every time I finish a combo and topple a hundred enemies in one go.

On the completion side of things, this game is in the middle of the spectrum. There are only 3 main quest logs: The Dramatic Log which is the story mode where you play as a select set of characters each quest, the Free Log which allows you to replay Dramatic Log missions with any character you want, and the ratings you get for each quest is shared between the two logs, and finally, the Treasure Log, where you'll probably spend most of your time because it has a whole lot of quests that when completed will reward you with golden coins that you need to level up your characters skills or stats.

Speaking of which, the Growth Maps offer a decent method of progressing your characters through buffing their main stats or unlocking new abilities for them. You can choose up to 4 abilities for these characters to use during each battle but the number of abilities you can unlock makes it so you have options in case you wish to change up your play style whenever you want. The only thing that bothers me is that you have to select a mission first before you can access the Growth Map, which isn't much of a problem since you can still navigate between different characters' maps, it's just a tedious process is all. I'm hoping that in a future patch the devs will add a Growth Map option to the main menu just to make it easier to access.

Oh, right, I almost forgot. The graphics of the game are pretty good. They're not incredible or realistic to any measure, but they do the job of representing a CGI anime game. The action cutscenes are definitely incredible though. It feels like a trip down memory lane but also a whole new experience at the same time. 

All in all, I give this game a good ol' 9/10. It's incredibly fun and can get addicting if you're not careful. I mean, look at me, I played 12 hours of this on launch day alone. That's dangerous, but it's a damn good time. Anyway, that's all I got for you. If you read all that, thank you first of all, and I genuinely hope you give this game a try. As a One Piece and Musou game fan, this brings me so much joy. Can't wait for the DLC characters!

[b] One Piece fans & Warriors players: [/b] 9.0/10
[b] Casual players & non-fans: [/b] 7.5/10
[h3] What OPPW4 does best is, ironically, built to a significant extent around the assumption that you already know One Piece. [/h3]
If [b] OPPW3 [/b] feels more like a [i] “One Piece museum” [/i]—or perhaps a [i] “One Piece chronicle” [/i]—then [b] OPPW4 [/b] feels much more like a [i] “One Piece power-fantasy action game.” [/i] It clearly shifts its focus toward combat, characters, spectacle, and the sheer fun of beating the hell out of everything in your path. In my opinion, it does all of these things better than any other game in the series, without question.

The trade-off, of course, is that the story is told in a very compressed manner.

This is something I want to emphasize: [b] if you're a newcomer who simply wants to get a general understanding of the One Piece story through a game, or if you're already a One Piece fan but care more about the quality of the narrative experience, I would recommend playing the previous game, OPPW3, without hesitation. [/b] It offers a relatively comprehensive retelling of the story up through the Dressrosa arc.

OPPW4, meanwhile, is the game in the series that, in my opinion, most clearly demonstrates the gap between the perspectives of a One Piece fan and a newcomer. Different groups of players can have radically different reactions depending on what they value:

How satisfying is the combat?
How distinct are the characters from one another?
How good is the new aerial combat system?
How many playable characters are there?
How good is the presentation?
How faithfully does it recreate the original?
How well does it capture iconic moments?
How is the story?
How fresh does it feel?
And so on...

Across these categories, I naturally rate the game much higher as a [b] One Piece fan + Warriors player [/b] than I would as a [b] non-fan + average player [/b].

I think OPPW4 is best described as a [b] fan-oriented game [/b]. Or, more precisely, it's a game that understands how to make the most of the [i] One Piece [/i] IP and, more importantly, knows exactly which aspects of the series translate best into a fun video game experience—and then goes all-in on them.

It does this extremely well. [b] It understands what we, as One Piece fans, actually want to see and play [/b].

That said, I also tried to look at the game from the perspective of someone who has no emotional attachment to One Piece: [i] If you strip away the appeal of the IP itself, how good is the game on its own [/i]?

My answer is still: [b] it's not bad, but it's nowhere near as good [/b].

If an average newcomer can reasonably give it a 7.5, while the same game can provide a 9.0 experience to fans because of its connection to a specific IP, I don't see that as a flaw. [b] That's precisely where the value of an IP-based game adaptation lies [/b].

As a result, the experience can be completely different depending on what kind of player you are.

If you're a newcomer and you see a particular scene from the game, you might simply think:

“[i] Oh, that's pretty cool. [/i]”

But if you're a One Piece fan, all it takes is seeing that same scene—even if the game itself renders it somewhat crudely—and your brain can automatically fill in an entire history of experiences:

[b] the game footage → memories of the original → the emotions you felt back then → the character's journey → iconic moments → the continuity of all the time you've spent following One Piece [/b]...

All of those emotions become compressed into a single, incredibly concentrated moment.

Combine that with OPPW4's satisfying, over-the-top gameplay, and the emotional value you get out of the experience is something a newcomer simply [b] cannot replicate [/b].

[hr][/hr]
[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
For newcomers, there are certainly plenty of problems to point out: repetitive missions, a lack of strategic depth, heavily compressed storytelling, and relatively monotonous level design.

As I mentioned above, [b] if you're primarily interested in the story, I'd recommend playing OPPW3 instead [/b].

For One Piece fans, however, the question we actually care about is much simpler:

[b] Did this game succeed in turning the One Piece we love into something we can actually experience for ourselves [/b]?

If that's the question, then my answer is an unequivocal [b] yes [/b].

Not only does it accomplish that goal—it does it [b] beautifully [/b].

And honestly, that's already enough for me to wholeheartedly recommend this game to every One Piece fan.

[hr][/hr]
[i] [b] A little side note [/b]

I've always hoped that, once One Piece is finally completed, we'll eventually get a game that tells the entire story from beginning to end in one continuous experience.

Unfortunately, that day may still be a very, very long way off.

As I'm writing this review, the original manga is still in the [b] Elbaf Arc. [/b] Speaking of which, perhaps, if OPPW5 ever happens, we'll even get to see [b] Imu [/b] make an appearance.

If there is a fifth game, that is. [/i]

A middle of the road musou game. I've played worse, but a lot better too. There's a lot of cool stuff here, but there's also a lot of annoyances and tedium too. 

Positives

1. This game is frequently on sale for dirt cheap. If you want to try this game, for the love of god wait for a sale. It is almost always less than $10 dollars for the basic edition, which more than justifies it's asking price. 

2. The cast of playable characters is extremely varied and well put together. A lot of musou games cut corners by having lots of clone characters or a shared weapon system for the cast. While there are a handful of sort-of-clones here, the overwhelming majority of characters all have unique basic and special attacks that often make them play completely differently from anyone else. While this does result in the roster being very unbalanced, with some characters being absurdly more powerful than others, almost all the characters are at least interesting to play.

3. The game scales well for a variety of machines. This developer is notorious for poor optimization on PC, but I was able to get satisfactory performance and visuals on both desktop and the ROG Ally with everything still looking great. I had a little initial trouble getting my xbox controller to work, but this was easily sorted in the steam settings. Overall this game looks great and runs at 60 fps even on middle of the road machines. 

4. The combat is flashy and impactful. The basic musou weak-strong attack combo system has been further expanded to include air combos and a customizable palette of special moves that can all be linked together fluidly. As an added bonus, environmental destruction is a prominent feature here, with entire buildings crumbling to rubble form your errant attacks. These features all ramp up the power fantasy aspect of these games to new levels, making you feel like an unstoppable juggernaut who can reduce entire cities to dust. 

Negatives

1. The story presentation is atrocious. Of course this was going to be a cliff notes summary of the One Piece saga at best, I expected that, but what really surprised me was how slapped together the story segments actually feel. Still images, pre-rendered scenes, and footage that seems to be lifted straight from previous games are often mashed together in overly lengthy lore-dump sequence. It just feels like a lot of corners were cut here, and the most laughable example was the refusal to give Iceburg an in-game character model for the Water 7 sequences. All of his dialogue just comes from somewhere off-screen while the characters stand around staring at nothing. It's bizarre and unintentionally hilarious at the same time. Also, once again, there is no English voice acting in this game. For most Japanese games this isn't a problem, but it is almost impossible to follow the dialogue for half a dozen characters quickly barking orders at you in the middle of combat.

2. Named characters are very annoying to fight. By default all enemy officers have a super-armor meter you have to first deplete in order for them to stagger and take increased damage. The problem is that as soon as you do this, without fail, most named characters will activate their full-burst ability, buffing their attack and allowing them to repeatedly ragdoll your character. A few of the characters, such as Crocodile and Kizaru, are also invincible while in this state and will force you to deplete their super-armor a second time to stop it, all while they constantly blast you away with massive AOE attacks. The game overall isn't particularly difficult, but for me the fun fell off a cliff every time I had to deal with one of these assholes. 

3. Progression is pretty mediocre. You don't gain experience or level up in this game, but instead have to spend collectible coins and money to purchase raw stat boosts and abilities for each character. This system was fine overall, but I was a bit disappointed that the power ceiling felt relatively low for a Musou game. Once you're 10 hours in or so it doesn't take much effort to max out a character, and once you've filled out their ability map that's pretty much it. A dlc was recently rolled out that introduced a new progression system where you collect and spend souls for infinitesimally small stat boosts, but the currency for this is an extremely rare drop unless you own a particular dlc pack that lets you earn them more easily. Considering that a lot of other Musou games let you become ridiculously overpowered with levels in the hundreds, late game progression here just felt tame and underwhelming in comparison. 

Overall, pretty cool game, get it on sale if you are a musou or One Piece fan.

8/10 - Not a perfect One Piece tribute, but Musou games have never been better. Full review below.

= Intro =

Love 'Musou' games, love One Piece. Recently started playing Berserk again, really looked forward to this after the letdown of DOOM: Eternal.

= Gameplay = 

It's a Musou. You play an absurdly powerful hero and beat up literally thousands of enemies with a variety of splashy attacks and combos, while conquering territory to spawn thousands of your own troops.

PW3 was a lot of fun, but felt floaty, repetitive and bland at times. Fortunately PW4 fixes a whole lot of that - combat is meatier, the new specials system is a fantastic improvement, boss fights are now fully realized and have some interesting mechanics (although Pica in particular reveals one of the game's biggest remaining flaws) and you even have a rudimentary skill tree - although not quite as good as Berserk's loot/crafting system. 

Story mode is solid, with a few caveats - and the Treasure Log (similar to the Dream/Nightmare log of the previous game) is a huge improvement, with some genuinely creative and fun mission goals.

Characters are well designed and varied, with each one having a unique mechanic or two. 

Honestly, gameplay wise there isn't much to complain about here. As a Musou, this feels like the genre is heading towards some point where it's going to explode into the mainstream.

Everything feels like an upgrade - maps are bigger, enemies are more plentiful, tons of little refinements and improvements all over the place. As a game, it's really good.

That said, there are some issues. I don't like having to play through the story to unlock the majority of characters - in the previous game you could earn them gradually through the Log mode. 

I don't like how much content the game skips over (more below) and the difficulty settings feel out of whack. Hard is great - if you don't mind a bit of grinding and a *huge* difficulty spike midway through, Normal is 'my first Musou game' and Easy is 'my drunk cat's first Musou game'. 

= Graphics & Audio =

While it's not going to knock your socks off, it's a much prettier game (and a great PC port) - with stuff like tesselation adding a lot of visual oomph. The game does look slightly washed out, but pumping up the vibrancy with something like Reshade works well.

However, the camera - a common problem in Musous is really bad here. The inclusion of gigantic enemies makes it worse, when the camera zooms out and starts clipping into the boss, the scenery etc. It's been a problem for a while in the genre, and the general excellence of the game makes it more obvious over time.

Music is solid, but I turned it off after a while. 

= Style =

This is where PW4 comes a bit short. As a game, on it's own merits, it's great. As a One Piece tribute, it's...complicated. Rather than focusing on the *entire* story of OP, PW4 instead cuts things down and focuses more on depth within each arc. However, this feels a little odd sometimes - so many really great bits of the story are cut here. No Skypeia, no Thriller Bark, no Impel Down, no Zou, no Fishman Island. And yes, this means that most of the characters from these arcs are cut too - no Enel, Moria, Magellan etc.

The real shame though is that the later arcs that PW3 didn't get to also feel a bit thin. Whole Cake island is done decently, but Dressrosa is ridiculously cut down - the only Doflamingo Family characters are Diamante and Pica (neither are playable). No Trebol, no Baby 5, no Gladius and you never get to play Greenbit, the underground docks etc. Meh.

If they wanted to cut redundant content and focus on newer stuff, why not cut Alabasta and give us a more fully realized version of Dressrosa?

Beyond this, there are a few fully realized characters in the game that are not playable - evidently being kept back for DLC. I despise DLC in a AAA priced game like this.

= Value =

There is a *lot* of game here. 36 main story missions (although it's more like 30, as quite a few of these are just boss fights. Beyond this, you've got the excellent new Treasure Log to play, online features etc. Definitely good value even at a AAA price - although, again, I dislike how much was cut and the evident DLC shenanigans going on here.

I do wish skill trees were a bit more fleshed out, but with a cast of 40+ characters, that may be a bit ambitious.

= Overall =

+ The best Musou game to date.
+ Insanely fun.
+ Plenty of content.
+ Lots of improvements and added features.
+ I'm already stoked for #5

- A huge amount of the OP story is missing here.
- Giant characters are not implemented well.
- Horrible camera.

At the end of the day, this game just...rocks. It's not a perfect One Piece game, but it's fairly close to a perfect Musou. Highly recommended, but if you are in it purely as a OP tribute, you may be let down.

Title: One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 

Introduction:
One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4, developed by Omega Force and published by Bandai Namco Entertainment, is the latest installment in the action-packed One Piece Warrior series. Set in the vast and vibrant world of Eiichiro Oda's popular manga and anime series, this game offers fans an immersive experience filled with intense battles, iconic characters, and a compelling storyline.

Graphics and Visuals:
Visually, One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 is a treat for fans and newcomers alike. The cel-shaded art style perfectly captures the essence of the anime, bringing beloved characters to life with vibrant colors and fluid animations. The attention to detail in character design and the dynamic environments contribute to an engaging and visually appealing gaming experience.

Gameplay:
The core gameplay of Pirate Warriors 4 remains faithful to its hack-and-slash roots, offering players a fast-paced and exhilarating combat system. Players can choose from a vast roster of characters, each with unique abilities and signature moves. The game introduces the "Musou" action style, allowing players to unleash devastating combo attacks on hordes of enemies. The inclusion of cooperative play adds an extra layer of enjoyment, letting players team up to tackle challenging missions together.

Storyline:
The game follows the One Piece storyline, taking players through major arcs of the manga. While the narrative may not offer new content for those already familiar with the series, it serves as an excellent introduction for newcomers. The engaging cutscenes and character interactions contribute to an immersive storytelling experience, capturing the essence of the beloved source material.

Character Roster and Progression:
One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 boasts an extensive roster of playable characters, including fan favorites like Luffy, Zoro, and Nami. Each character has a unique playstyle and special moves, providing variety and replay value. The progression system allows players to upgrade their characters, unlocking new abilities and enhancing their combat prowess. This adds a strategic element to the gameplay, encouraging players to experiment with different characters and playstyles.

Music and Sound:
The game's soundtrack complements the high-energy gameplay, featuring iconic tunes from the anime series. The voice acting, available in both English and Japanese, adds authenticity to the characters, making it an enjoyable experience for fans who prefer the original voice cast.

Conclusion:
One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 successfully combines the beloved world of One Piece with the thrilling gameplay of the Warriors series. With its stunning visuals, diverse character roster, and engaging combat system, it offers an enjoyable experience for both fans of the franchise and action game enthusiasts. Whether you're a Straw Hat Pirate veteran or a newcomer setting sail for the first time, this game promises an exciting and swashbuckling adventure in the world of One Piece.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
One Piece Pirate Worries 4 is based on the hit anime [b]One Piece[/b] and is the predecessors of the three other games in the series. Combat is played the same, however, it is tweaked and is more smooth and air combat is much better as well. The game is sure to keep fans of [b]One Piece[/b], both casual and hardcore invested with its wonderful gameplay and retelling of the story.  

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[h3]Pros[/h3]
+ A great retelling of the [b]One Piece[/b] story.
+ Fun gameplay that can sometimes even be addictive
+ Both casual and hardcore [b]One Piece[/b] fans can find enjoyment in this game
+ Over 43 different characters to play as, plus a season pass with some more.
+ Four different subtypes to play as.

[h3]Cons[/h3]
- Gameplay may get stale for some people. 
- Some fan-favorite arks did not make it into the game.
- Some of the characters that were playable in OPW3 are not playable in this game. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game’s story follows the anime’s story and plays it through arks with a few levels in each and every word. The story of One Piece is great and the game tells it very well with the arks that we have been giving, the story has the One Piece charm and that is something that all fans can enjoy. 

However, not all arks made it into the game and fan favorites were removed as well. The entire [b]East Blue Saga[/b] was cut, the game starts at [b]Alabasta[/b], so no [b]Drum Island ark[/b], [b]Skypiea[/b] was removed, [b]Thriller Bark[/b], [b]Impel Down[/b], [b]Fish-Man Island[/b], and [b]Punk Hazard[/b] were also removed. This is disappointing, mainly because a lot of [b]One Piece[/b] fans loved some of these arks. [b]Enel[/b] and [b]Magellan[/b] were not even shown in the story or mentioned, however, [b]Gecko Moria[/b] was shown once in the story when the game was talking about [b]Thriller Bark[/b]. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay in the game is very fun and can be addictive at times as well, there are many characters for you to select sometimes depending on the mission you are giving. Each character has its own moves and has one of the four subtypes, Power, Speed, Technique, and Sky. Some characters can be a certain subtype in the Pre-time skip but have different moves in the Post-time Skip due to certain transformations, for example, Sanji is a speed type in the Pre-time skip but at the Post-time skip, he will be a Sky type due to some of his moves been modified.  

Every character has three special moves and a mode where they can be powered up and do extra damage. Most of these special moves will take out most enemies and will do a large chunk of damage to bosses. At some point, characters will enter a [b]Full-Force Burst[/b] mode, when this mode is activated they will get a special benefit depending on their subtype. 

[h3]Power Types[/h3]
Power Types are centered around the fact that they can deal large amounts of damage and take out enemies very quickly. When a power type character is hit by an enemy, a wall, or the floor, a shock wave is sent out and will damage any enemies that are near it. When power types are in [b]Full-Force Burst[/b], they will get more attack damage and their smash attacks are more powerful.  

[h3]Speed Types[/h3]
Speed types are more focused on combat as they have combo potential, and they can move around very fast, their stamina usage is also reduced in a power dash. When Speed types are in [b]Full-Force Burst[/b], their stamina usage is greatly reduced in a power dash. 

[h3]Technique Types[/h3]
Technique types are the most interesting as they have special moves that affect gameplay, like putting enemies to sleep, using oil, and lighting it up to make fire, and there is so much more. Technique types can also perform an attack while charging that will push enemies towards them. When a Technique type enters [b]Full-Force Burst[/b] their special traits of that character are powered up.  

[h3]Sky Types[/h3]
Sky types are a bit weird at first but they focus on air combat and have the most characteristics out of all the types. They are immune to all damage during a power dash, their power dash counties until all the stamina is used up, enemies that are not on the ground can get caught up in their power dash, and they can use stamina to start an attack when falling from an aerial attack. When a Sky type goes [b]Full-Force Burst[/b], they will have the ability to float constantly and their stamina usage is decreased during a power dash.  

[h1]Combat[/h1]
Combat is like other [b]Dynasty Worries[/b] games and the main objective for every single mission is to beat up a bunch of enemies, beat up leaders to take over territories to get more minions to help you fight. At some point, you will fight a mini-boss or a boss, when bosses come out they will have an [b]Armor Gauge[/b] if you remove all of the [b]Armor Gauge[/b] they will be stunned and put into a state called [b]Armor Break State[/b], in which they will take more damage.
Depending on who you fight, that characters [b]Devil Fruit[/b] may come into play as well if the character has one of course. [b]Peramecia[/b] and [b]Zeons[/b] don’t really have any gimmicks when it comes to attacking them other than the fact that their devil fruit is their move set mostly. However, if a Logia activates their ability, their appearance can change and normal attacks will not harm them. To harm someone with a Logia they will need to be put in their armor break state and all attacks will harm them when they are in this state.

[h3]Sub-Missions[/h3]
Sometimes a [b]Sub-Mission[/b] may take place during the level at a certain location or if you do certain requirements, these [b]Sub-Missions[/b] can be things like normal missions as well when the time comes for them. If you are able to complete these missions, then you will get rewarded barries which is the currency for the game.  

[h1]Dreamlog[/h1]
[b]Dreamlog[/b] is a mode that lets you play a bunch of missions, in this mode, you can get barries that help you level up your characters. [b]Dream log[/b] has you do the same missions as what the story mode provides but it’s mostly just you fighting a bunch of enemies, you will have different characters that will team up with you. You can play as any character in this mode if you have them unlocked, some character can only be unlocked in [b]Dreamlog[/b] after completing certain missions. 

[h1]What Holds The Game Back[/h1]
The gameplay is fun but it can get stale sometimes, especially after you are done completing the story. [b]Dream Log[/b] is a nice feature but you are doing the same thing over and over again and there is really no motive to continue playing. 

[h1]Preformance[/h1]
I was able to play the game in high settings, I used a NIVIDA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, 16 GB of RAM storage on a 2560:1440 [16:9] monitor. The game runs really smooth and I had no issues what so ever while playing, the game may look like you need a good computer, but if you have a decent computer, you should be able to run the game in low settings.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
One Piece Pirate Worries 4 is a great addition to the series and is a wonderfully made game, I have been an avid player of the previous game and this one proves once again why this series is great. Fans of the series can look forward to more of what they’ve come to love and expect.

Saying it's worse than Pirate Warriors 3 is like saying a banana split with chocolate syrup on it is worse than a banana split with butterscotch syrup on it. You're still getting a banana split, it's still delicious, and it's really all down to personal taste.

This game slaps, but I'm a butterscotch kinda guy. One thing I really don't like about it, though it's not a game breaker, is how much looser the combat feels compared to its predecessors -- you really feel like, especially with speed and sky-type characters, you're just zooming around almost to the point of being out of control. I haven't played as all of the characters yet, so I can't really say I've settled into one I enjoy deeply, but as a result I'm finding myself playing as a wider variety of characters compared to earlier titles *because* I haven't settled into a main. The characters I usually play as have been changed dramatically (Sanji) or gutted to an unfortunate degree (Tashigi), so finding a new one is a bit of an ongoing effort, I'd say.

The campaign mode is fine, it's about as good as any of the PW games' campaigns are, though I really do miss PW1's more linear, mission-type layouts with obstacles to overcome and problems to solve compared to later games' more traditional musou play. I didn't realize how much I missed that kind of musou game until I played P5 Strikers, actually. PW4 being a more traditional musou game like PW3 but without the *impact* you feel with your attacks and without some real army-clearing attacks like the Kizuna follow-ups makes it feel a lot less dynamic as a result. The fact that there's not much free-play or mission mode like PW3's is also a point against it.

But, where the game falters is also where it really kicks up something new and interesting by comparison. If you're a grindfest kinda guy like I am, the new character upgrade maps are a treat and make you feel like you're really advancing a character unlike PW3's coin system. The giant enemies are fun as heck to take down even on harder difficulties, where you'd expect them to just be HP sponges, and they add a layer of strategy to the greater map design that I really enjoyed. Overall, I would say the feeling of taking down a giant and capturing territories in this game is about as fun and high-pressure as getting Kizuna score was in PW3, and I'm a lot more thankful of how much less stressful S-Ranking a map is in this one.

Barebones PC port with 60fps lock, no default options for wide screen, no option to run in windowed mode (game will run over all other windows unless you alt+tab to another window), and limited options to tweak display settings based on hardware. However, it ran well on a 5700x3d + 9060xt +32GB RAM configuration with no crashes in 30 or so hours of gameplay.

Gameplay style involves heavy button mashing which may cause repetitive strain injury to develop - this can be somewhat managed by adjusting your controller to repeatedly press one button when the button is held down.

The base game content is generous with 43 characters, although the 100 stages offered are often simply different sets of objectives that start you on a different point of the map. Only one map is somewhat frustrating as it contains 5 levels, with no way to check which floor you are on or to view the map three dimensionally.

The game's adaptation of the source material is highly abridged, with some story points that are exclusive to the game. However, the narrative is mostly serviceable and straightforward enough for players to follow.

Multiplayer component for up to four players online, as well as 2 player offline co-op, is present; however multiplayer features were not tested or used.
